items.prompt: What is "progressive delivery"?
choices: The general practice of rolling out a change gradually and monitoring at each stage, rather than shipping to all users at once
A specific brand of continuous integration software that competing vendors license from one another
The practice of writing unusually detailed release notes for every single deploy, however small
A deployment strategy that always requires manual sign-off and approval from a company director
items.explanation: Progressive delivery is specifically about gradual, monitored rollout — not a specific software product, documentation practice, or approval hierarchy.

items.prompt: Does progressive delivery prevent bugs that only surface under real production traffic?
choices: No — it doesn't prevent this category of bug; it changes how many users are exposed to it before it's caught
Yes — progressive delivery is described as guaranteeing such bugs are caught before affecting any user at all
No, and on top of that it's described as providing no real benefit for this specific kind of bug
Yes, but the described benefit only applies to bugs related specifically to database performance
items.explanation: L1 is explicit that progressive delivery doesn't prevent production-only bugs — its value is limiting exposure, not prevention.

items.prompt: What is a "canary deployment"?
choices: Routing a small, defined percentage of production traffic to a new version, then expanding the percentage in stages if the canary shows no problems
A deployment that, by long-standing team convention, only ever happens on weekends to minimize overall risk
A deployment strategy that specifically requires two completely separate engineering teams to sign off on it first
A backup deployment process kept on standby that only ever activates automatically if the primary one fails outright
items.explanation: Canary deployment is specifically about gradual traffic percentage — not scheduling, approval processes, or failover backups.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, would a canary deployment starting at 5% have prevented the bug from existing in the code?
choices: No — it wouldn't prevent the bug from existing, but it would limit how many users encountered it before it was caught
Yes — canary deployments are described in L1 as guaranteeing fully bug-free code before a full rollout
No, and beyond that, canary deployments are described as providing no benefit in this scenario at all
Yes, but only in the case where the canary stage is kept running for longer than 24 hours
items.explanation: A canary deployment doesn't fix the underlying bug — it limits exposure to it while it's being detected, which is the core value described in L1.

items.prompt: What is "blue-green deployment"?
choices: Running two complete, identical production environments, where traffic is switched entirely from one to the other, allowing an instant switch back
A deployment strategy whose name simply comes from the two most common company brand colors used historically
A technique for gradually increasing the percentage of live traffic sent to a new version over time instead
A monitoring dashboard whose panels are merely color-coded green or red according to overall service health
items.explanation: Blue-green is specifically about two parallel environments and instant traffic switching — not branding, gradual percentage rollout, or dashboards.

items.prompt: Per L1, would blue-green deployment alone have limited how many users hit the Scenario's bug before it was noticed?
choices: No — blue-green makes rollback fast once a bug is noticed, but doesn't limit how many users are exposed before that point
Yes — blue-green deployment is described as guaranteeing that zero users are ever exposed to a new bug
Yes, but only in the specific case where the two environments run on identical underlying hardware
No, and blue-green deployment is described as providing no benefit whatsoever in the Scenario
items.explanation: L1/L2 distinguish blue-green's rollback-speed benefit from canary's exposure-limiting benefit — they solve different parts of the problem.

items.prompt: What is a "feature flag"?
choices: A runtime toggle that controls whether a piece of code is active, allowing a feature to be turned off instantly without a new deploy
A short comment left inline in source code that simply marks an old section of it as deprecated for cleanup
A command-line flag passed to a build tool purely to enable a more verbose level of console logging output
A small visual marker shown in a UI indicating to end users that a given feature is still in beta
items.explanation: A feature flag is specifically a runtime toggle independent of deploys — not a code comment, build flag, or UI badge.

items.prompt: How does a feature flag's mechanism differ from a canary deployment's mechanism?
choices: A feature flag toggles whether code runs at all, independent of the deployed version, while canary controls what percentage of traffic reaches a different version
They are, in practical terms, functionally identical mechanisms that simply go by two different marketing names
A feature flag is described as something usable only inside a staging environment, never in live production traffic
A canary deployment is described as structurally requiring feature flags to be present in order to function at all
items.explanation: L1 draws a real mechanical distinction: feature flags gate code execution at runtime, while canary routes traffic between deployed versions — related but not the same lever.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, could the bug have reliably been caught by tests or staging before production?
choices: No — the Scenario states it only showed up under real production traffic patterns that staging couldn't fully replicate
Yes — the Scenario explicitly states the bug was actually caught during staging testing but then ignored anyway
Yes, but only because the team is described as having skipped their staging environment entirely that cycle
It's impossible to tell from the Scenario's stated facts whether staging could plausibly have caught it
items.explanation: The Scenario explicitly frames this as a bug category that only surfaces under real production conditions, not one that better testing alone would have caught.

items.prompt: Given that the bug wasn't reliably testable beforehand, what does L1 suggest was actually avoidable about the Scenario's incident?
choices: Whether shipping to 100% of traffic at once, rather than a smaller percentage first, was necessary
The existence of the bug itself, which L1 claims was fully preventable
Nothing was avoidable — the Scenario describes a purely unavoidable incident
The 20 minutes it took to diagnose the problem, which L1 claims should have been instantaneous
items.explanation: L1's closing question specifically targets the decision to ship to 100% of traffic at once, not the bug's existence or the exact diagnosis time.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does canary deployment control that blue-green deployment doesn't?
choices: How many users are exposed to a new version before it's fully rolled out
How fast a full rollback can happen once a bug is noticed
Whether a specific piece of code runs at all
The physical region where a service is hosted
items.explanation: L2's table attributes exposure control specifically to canary, not to blue-green (which controls rollback speed instead).

items.prompt: Per L2, does blue-green deployment limit how many users hit a bug before someone notices and switches back?
choices: No — L2 explicitly lists this as something blue-green doesn't solve
Yes — limiting user exposure before detection is described as blue-green's core purpose
Yes, but only for deployments smaller than a certain traffic volume
No, and L2 states blue-green provides no safety benefit of any kind
items.explanation: L2's table explicitly lists 'doesn't limit how many users hit a bug before someone notices' under blue-green's column — that's canary's job, not blue-green's.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, what happens at each stage of a staged canary rollout?
choices: A real health check gates whether the rollout advances to the next percentage or halts and rolls back
The rollout automatically advances to the next stage after a fixed amount of time, with no health check
Each stage requires a completely new deployment from scratch
Traffic percentage decreases at each stage until reaching zero
items.explanation: L2's diagram shows each stage gated by a genuine health signal (healthy → advance, unhealthy → halt/roll back) — not a timer alone, a fresh redeploy, or decreasing percentages.

items.prompt: Per L2, why not start a canary rollout at 50% instead of 5%, to reach full rollout faster?
choices: The point is limiting exposure while the signal is still uncertain — starting small means a bug caught at the first stage affects the fewest possible users
Starting a canary rollout at 50% is described as technically impossible with current canary deployment infrastructure
Starting at a higher percentage always produces a slower overall deployment, regardless of how monitoring is set up
There's no real reason given — L2 states starting at 50% would be exactly as safe as starting at 5%
items.explanation: L2 explicitly ties the small starting percentage to limiting exposure during the period of highest uncertainty — not to a technical limitation or an unexplained rule.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's wrong with treating any one of canary, blue-green, or feature flags as covering all three purposes?
choices: Each solves a different part of the problem — blue-green without canary still exposes 100% of traffic to a new bug immediately, just with a faster fix once found
There's no real issue described at all — any single one of the three techniques is treated as fully sufficient alone
This gap is framed in L2 as being a problem only for companies with fewer than ten total engineers on staff
The issue L2 actually raises here is purely about licensing cost, not about any real gap in risk coverage
items.explanation: L2 explicitly warns against treating the techniques as interchangeable — each addresses a distinct failure mode, and skipping one leaves that specific risk unaddressed.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's the risk of a canary stage that only checks "did the server crash"?
choices: It misses a subtle correctness bug that doesn't crash anything, just quietly returns wrong results — exactly the Scenario's failure mode
There's no risk at all — crash-only monitoring is described in L2 as sufficient for catching any kind of bug
The risk is framed as applying only to serverless deployments specifically, never to traditional long-running servers
Crash-only monitoring is actually described in L2 as overly cautious and therefore generally unnecessary
items.explanation: L2 explicitly ties this failure mode back to the Scenario's own bug — a correctness issue that a crash-only check would never catch.

items.prompt: Fix assignVersion so it deterministically and consistently routes users whose hash bucket is below canaryPercent to "new". Across many users this approximates the rollout percentage, while keeping each user's assignment stable.

tests.description: at 0% canary, every user gets the old version
at 100% canary, every user gets the new version
the same user gets the same version every time at a fixed percentage

items.explanation: Hashing the user id into a fixed 0-99 bucket and comparing against the canary percentage gives both determinism (same input, same bucket, always) and percentage control by bucket threshold. Real user counts can be approximate, but the routing rule is stable and needs no per-user state.
items.reference:
🎲 Deterministic hash — same user id always maps to the same bucket
📊 Threshold — moving it changes which buckets get routed to "new"

Why: a canary rollout needs both properties at once — controllable exposure, and a stable per-user experience.

items.prompt: Fix shouldHaltRollout so it correctly computes the error rate as a percentage and compares it against the threshold, handling zero total requests safely.

tests.description: halts when the error rate exceeds the threshold (3% > 2%)
does not halt when the error rate is within the threshold (1% <= 2%)
does not halt when there are zero total requests yet

items.explanation: Converting to a rate (not an absolute count) is what makes this check meaningful at any canary size — 30 errors out of 1,000 canary requests is a real 3% signal, while 30 errors would mean something completely different out of a million requests.
items.reference:
🔢 Absolute count — meaningless without knowing the traffic volume it came from
📈 Rate — comparable against a fixed threshold regardless of canary size

Why: a small canary stage needs a rate-based check to catch a real problem without waiting for a large absolute error count.
